The Delagoa threadfin bream (Nemipterus bipunctatus) attains a maximum recorded standard length of 30 centimeters [Li = 30 centimeters] in its natural habitat across the western Indian Ocean. This ultimate length, characteristic of a moderately sized demersal predator within the Nemipteridae, is typically reached after several years of sustained somatic growth on the continental shelf. Field surveys conducted along the coasts of Mozambique and Somalia indicate that individuals achieving this size are relatively rare, likely due to size-selective fishing pressure on older cohorts. The species exhibits a clear allometric relationship between length and mass, with the maximum adult body mass estimated at 297 grams [Wwi = 297 grams] for a 30 centimeter fish. This mass-length relationship underscores a robust, laterally compressed body form suited for maneuvering among coral rubble and seagrass beds. Comparisons with related species from the same genus suggest that Nemipterus bipunctatus is intermediate in both asymptotic length and weight relative to its Indian Ocean congeners, falling below the larger Nemipterus japonicus but exceeding smaller-bodied species such as Nemipterus marginatus.

Sexual maturation in this species is initiated once individuals reach a standard length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters], a size that corresponds to approximately half their ultimate length. At this pubertal stage, the corresponding body mass is approximately 38 grams [Wwp = approximately 38 grams], derived from the length-weight relationship established for local populations. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from trawl-caught specimens reveals that the onset of vitellogenesis and spermiation occurs synchronously with the attainment of this size threshold, typically during the late spring months when water temperatures begin to rise. This early maturation strategy, whereby reproduction commences at roughly half the maximum length, is common among small-to-medium-sized nemipterids and reflects a life history that prioritizes early reproductive output over prolonged somatic investment. The standard length at puberty of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters] also serves as a useful reference point for fisheries managers, providing a biological basis for minimum size limits intended to protect immature individuals from harvest before they have had the opportunity to spawn at least once.

Reproductive output in Nemipterus bipunctatus has been inferred from detailed studies on the closely related congener Nemipterus japonicus, and these estimates are considered applicable under comparable thermal regimes. For a female measuring 23.75 centimeters in fork length, the annual fecundity is approximately 139200 eggs per female at a stable water temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C]. This substantial number reflects an iteroparous, multiple-batch spawning strategy typical of tropical nemipterids, with females spawning approximately 40 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 40 times per year], each event yielding roughly 3480 eggs [N_R_i = each event yielding roughly 3480 eggs]. This high fecundity, combined with a relatively early age at first reproduction, allows the species to maintain stable population densities despite natural and fishing-induced mortality. The decomposition into per-event fecundity and spawning frequency provides a critical parameter for understanding the species' demographic resilience under varying environmental conditions.

The earliest life stages of the Delagoa threadfin bream begin with the fertilized ova, which are small pelagic eggs approximately 0.5 millimeters in diameter. From this egg diameter, the wet weight at birth has been calculated as 0.000066 grams [Wwb = 0.000066 grams], representing the mass of the newly hatched yolk-sac larva upon eclosion from the chorion. This minute initial mass, equivalent to roughly 66 micrograms, is typical of marine teleosts that produce large numbers of small, planktonic offspring as part of a high-fecundity, low-investment reproductive strategy. The lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves during the first few days post-hatching, undergoing rapid morphological development including mouth opening and retinal differentiation before the onset of exogenous feeding. The tiny body mass at emergence imposes significant constraints on early larval survival, as the larvae must quickly locate and capture suitably sized microplanktonic prey to avoid starvation. This bottleneck at the first-feeding transition is a critical period in the early life history, and the extremely low birth weight of 0.000066 grams [Wwb = 0.000066 grams] highlights the vulnerability of the species at this stage.

Maximum longevity for Nemipterus bipunctatus has been estimated at approximately 6 years under natural conditions, based on otolith increment analysis of wild-caught specimens from the southeastern African coast. At the prevailing ambient water temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C], individuals are expected to complete their entire life cycle within this six-year span (6 years) [am = 6 years], with growth rates and metabolic demands closely tied to the warm, stable thermal environment of the tropical continental shelf. This lifespan is consistent with that reported for other medium-sized nemipterids in the region, which typically exhibit a life expectancy of between 5 and 8 years in the absence of heavy fishing pressure. The temperature of 26.1 °C [T = 26.1 °C] is representative of the mean annual sea surface temperature in the core of the species' distributional range, and it likely influences not only the rate of somatic growth but also the timing of gonadal recrudescence and spawning periodicity. Senescence in this species is accompanied by a gradual decline in reproductive output and body condition during the final year of life, with mortality typically occurring in the post-spawning period.
